turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm here because... well, for over a year now, I've been trying to get someone, anyone, to take it seriously. It's about work. The new ticket rotation and those security audits... they're being used to build a paper trail against me. Management keeps showing me these logs, you know, trying to brush it off, saying it's just standard policy. Policy! Ha. 

It reminds me of this one time back in the 90s, I was working this helpdesk job for a logistics firm, and they had this "policy" about how we logged our calls. Turns out, it was just a way to figure out who was spending too much time talking to the warehouse guys. I knew a guy there, Dave, he got let go because of it. Or maybe it was Steve... anyway, he had this incredible collection of vintage keyboards. I mean, the real clicky ones, IBM Model Ms. You don't see those much anymore, everyone wants those flat, silent things now. I actually rebuilt an old Model M last weekend, took me hours to get the springs just right... but yeah, the audits. They say it's policy, but I know what they're really doing.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient holds a fixed, persecutory belief that management is building a paper trail against them, despite being shown contradictory evidence (logs).
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, drifting from the topic of work audits to a past job, a former coworker, and vintage keyboards before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: When they show you the logs and say the audits are standard policy, do you believe that could be true?
turns.patient_response:
Could it be true? Well... no. Because I've been trying to get someone, anyone, to take this seriously for over a year now. They sit there in the office, they point at the monitor and show me these logs, and they keep saying it's just the new ticket rotation policy. But I know it's a paper trail against me. They're using those security audits to build a case. 

And you know, logs can be altered anyway. I used to write these parsing scripts in Perl back in the early 2000s that could rewrite a server log in a blink. Perl was fantastic for that. People always complained the syntax looked like gibberish, like someone just fell asleep on the keyboard, but if you really understood regular expressions... it was an art form, really. I had this one script I called the 'Librarian'. I kept it on this chunky little 128-megabyte thumb drive. Cost me an absolute fortune at Circuit City. You remember Circuit City? With the big red plug on the front of the building? I bought my first digital camera there, too. A two-megapixel Sony. Took it on a trip to Yellowstone... 

But, no, when management says it's standard policy, they're just covering up what they're actually doing to me.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices when no one else is around?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? No, no, I don't hear any voices. It's just the people at work talking, you know, whispering behind my back when they think I can't hear them. But actual voices out of nowhere? No. 

Though, speaking of hearing things, I did use to have this awful ringing in my ears back when I worked in the server room at that data center in '98. Those old rack-mount servers, the fans on them were like jet engines. We had this one row of Compaq ProLiants... they were these heavy, beige monsters. You had to practically be a bodybuilder to rack one of those things. I slipped a disc trying to lift one by myself once. Had to go to a chiropractor for six months. He had this weird machine with all these rolling massagers on it... felt like you were being kneaded like dough. But anyway, yeah, the noise in that server room was deafening. You'd step outside and your ears would just ring for hours. We were supposed to wear ear protection, but nobody ever did. You couldn't hear the pager go off if you had the earmuffs on, and back then, if you missed a page, it was your neck. 

But no, no voices or anything like that. Just the usual office noise, and... well, what management is trying to do to me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses suspicious beliefs that coworkers are whispering behind his back and that management is plotting against him, indicating persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices out of nowhere.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech by going off on a long, unrelated tangent about a server room in 1998, a chiropractor, and pagers before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had a period when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?
turns.patient_response:
Less sleep? Full of energy? No, not really. I mean, I sleep okay, I guess. Usually get my six or seven hours. 

Although, there was this one time back in the early 2000s, I pulled three all-nighters in a row during the Y2K transition. We were terrified the legacy mainframe was just going to completely brick itself at midnight. We had this huge stockpile of Mountain Dew and these terrible frozen burritos from the gas station down the street. I remember the microwave in the breakroom had this weird quirk where the turntable would only spin counter-clockwise, and it made this awful grinding noise. It was a Sharp Carousel, I think. My grandmother had a Sharp Carousel, but hers had this faux-wood paneling on the side. She used to make the most amazing apple butter in the fall. We'd go pick the apples at this orchard upstate... McIntosh apples, mostly. They're the best for cooking down because they get really soft. 

But anyway, no, I don't get those bursts of energy or anything. Just normal sleep for me. Unless I'm up worrying about what they're putting in those audit logs, of course.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits highly tangential speech, drifting from a story about Y2K to a microwave, their grandmother, and apple picking before returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies feeling full of energy or having bursts of energy.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies needing less sleep, stating they get their normal six or seven hours.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from this issue at work, have you had trouble functioning in your daily life?
turns.patient_response:
Trouble functioning? No, not at all. Outside of this whole mess with the ticket rotation and the audits, everything is fine. I still keep the house in order, pay the bills on time, help my wife out around the house. And honestly, I still handle the technical parts of my job perfectly fine. Nobody has ever said my actual work is sloppy or disorganized. 

Speaking of keeping things organized, my wife and I just reorganized the garage last weekend. We bought these heavy-duty plastic shelving units from Home Depot. The black ones, you know? They just snap together, no tools required. Though, I always use a rubber mallet just to make sure the joints are seated properly. I bought this mallet years ago at a flea market... it has a wooden handle that's worn perfectly smooth. The guy who sold it to me had this massive collection of vintage hand tools. He had these old Stanley hand planes that were just beautiful. Real craftsmanship, you know? Not like the cheap metal stuff they stamp out today. I used to do a little woodworking myself back in the nineties. Made a birdhouse for my mother's backyard. It was supposed to be a replica of a Victorian house, complete with little gingerbread trim around the roof. Took me weeks to cut all those tiny pieces with a scroll saw. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, functioning. Yeah, no problems there. I do my job, I take care of things at home. It's just... I have to stay vigilant about what management is doing behind my back.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any neurological illness or brain injury?
turns.patient_response:
Neurological illness? Brain injury? No, no, nothing like that. My brain works just fine, always has. 

Though, you know, speaking of heads, I did get a pretty nasty bump on mine back in... oh, it must have been '86. I was trying to install a ceiling fan in our first apartment. The instructions were completely useless, printed in this tiny font that looked like it had been photocopied a hundred times. I was balancing on this rickety wooden step stool my father-in-law gave us. It had these metal hinges that were rusted shut, so you could never quite lock the legs into place. Anyway, I lost my balance and smacked my head right on the edge of the drywall. Didn't black out or anything, just a big goose egg. 

My wife put a bag of frozen peas on it. We always kept a bag of those Green Giant peas in the freezer, not for eating, just for ice packs. They mold to the shape of your head perfectly. Much better than actual ice cubes, which always melt and leak water down your neck. We had this old Frigidaire refrigerator back then... avocado green, typical seventies color. The compressor on that thing was so loud, it sounded like a diesel engine starting up every time it kicked on. I tried to fix it once, bought a new relay switch from a parts store across town. The guy who ran the place had this massive greyhound dog that would just sleep on the counter all day. Beautiful dog, but completely lazy. 

But no, to answer your question, no brain injuries or neurological problems. My mind is sharp. It has to be, to keep track of all the subtle ways they're trying to push me out of my job.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a persecutory belief that others are subtly trying to push him out of his job.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits marked tangentiality, wandering from a head bump to a ceiling fan, frozen peas, a refrigerator, and a dog before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Has anything happened that makes you think management can do things that would be impossible for ordinary people to do?
turns.patient_response:
Impossible things? Like magic or something? No, no, they're just ordinary people. Sneaky, manipulative people, but just regular humans. They're just using the system against me, manipulating the ticket queues and the audit logs. Nothing supernatural. 

Though, speaking of impossible things, I did see David Copperfield live once. Vegas, maybe '94 or '95? We stayed at the Mirage. That was back when they had the white tigers right there in the lobby enclosure. Siegfried and Roy were still performing then. The whole strip was different back then, you know? Less corporate, more... I don't know, more character. We ate at this buffet that had a prime rib carving station that was just incredible. The chef had this massive chef's hat, the classic tall white one, and he wielded this carving knife that must have been eighteen inches long. He sharpened it on a steel right there in front of you. Shhhk, shhhk, shhhk. 

I actually bought a good set of Wüsthof knives after that trip. The Classic line, with the three rivets in the handle. They're forged in Solingen, Germany. You really have to hand wash them, though. If you put them in the dishwasher, the harsh detergent pits the high-carbon steel. My wife accidentally put the paring knife in the dishwasher once, and I spent an hour polishing it out with this special compound I ordered from a catalog. The catalog was one of those specialty cooking ones... Williams Sonoma, maybe? They used to send these thick, glossy catalogs right before the holidays. Always featured these perfect roast turkeys on the cover. 

But anyway, no, management isn't doing anything impossible. They're just very, very good at covering their tracks in the system.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses persecutory delusions, firmly believing that management is manipulating systems and audit logs against them, even while denying they have supernatural abilities.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, drifting from the topic of 'impossible things' into a long, loosely associated monologue about a Vegas trip, buffets, and kitchen knives before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Is it possible that you could be mistaken about management trying to build a case against you?
turns.patient_response:
Mistaken? No, I'm not mistaken. I mean, I'm here because for over a year now I've been trying to get someone to actually take this seriously. The new ticket rotation, the constant security audits... they are absolutely being used to build a paper trail against me. Management keeps pulling up these logs and trying to tell me, "Oh, it's just policy, it's standard procedure." But I know what I'm looking at. 

Speaking of logs, we used to keep an actual, physical logbook back when I started in IT. This was the early nineties. We had this thick, bound ledger... the kind with the marbled green and black cover and the pale green paper inside with the red lines. Every time a server went down, you had to write it in by hand with a pen. I always used a Pilot Precise V5. The extra fine point. They have that liquid ink that just glides over the paper. But you had to be careful, because if you paused for even a second, the ink would bleed right through the page. 

I bought a whole box of those pens at a Staples that was going out of business. The whole store was practically empty, just these bare metal shelves and a few sad-looking desk chairs marked down by eighty percent. I actually bought one of those chairs, too. It had this mesh back that was supposed to be ergonomic, but it really just dug into your shoulder blades. My wife ended up putting it out on the curb for bulk trash day. The trash guys in our neighborhood are great, though. They drive these massive automated trucks with the mechanical arm that just reaches out and grabs the bin. It's fascinating to watch. The hydraulics on those arms must be incredibly powerful to lift a full bin like it's nothing. 

But no, I'm not mistaken about management. They can show me all the logs they want and claim it's just policy, but I know they're building a case to get rid of me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed belief that management is building a case against them, explicitly rejecting the possibility of being mistaken despite contradictory evidence (management's logs and policy explanations).
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting off-topic from IT logs to specific pens, a closing Staples store, an uncomfortable chair, and finally garbage truck hydraulics.

turns.doctor_question: Before this problem at work started, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?
turns.patient_response:
Distrust other people's motives? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, generally speaking, I've always been pretty easygoing. I take people at face value, you know? Unless they give me a reason not to. 

Like my neighbor, Frank. We've lived next door to each other for fifteen years. He borrowed my pressure washer once, back in... oh, 2012 maybe? It was a Honda, gas-powered, 3100 PSI. Really good machine. I bought it specifically to clean the green algae off the north side of the house. You have to be careful with those gas ones, though, because if you get the nozzle too close to the siding, it'll strip the paint right off. Anyway, Frank borrowed it to do his driveway, and when he brought it back, he had completely drained the gas tank and didn't refill it. Just left it bone dry. 

I didn't say anything, of course, just went down to the Shell station on the corner with my red plastic jerry can. That gas station used to have a full-service island, if you can believe it. A guy would come out, pump your gas, check your oil, wash your windshield. They wore those neat little uniforms with the name patches. You don't see that anymore. Now it's all pay-at-the-pump with those little screens that are always broken or too glaring in the sun to read. And they play those loud advertisements at you while you're pumping. It's so intrusive. I always try to press the buttons on the side of the screen to mute it, but they must have disabled that feature on the new pumps. 

But no, before this whole mess at work, I didn't go around suspecting people. I just did my job, helped my users, and trusted that if I did good work, I'd be treated fairly. It's only recently, with all this targeted auditing, that I've had to start watching my back.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient refers to recent 'targeted auditing' at work and having to 'start watching my back,' which indicates the presence of persecutory delusions.

turns.doctor_question: What evidence would convince you that management is not trying to build a case against you?
turns.patient_response:
Evidence? I... I don't think there is any evidence that could convince me otherwise, because I've been dealing with this for over a year. I've been practically begging someone, anyone, to take this seriously. The new ticket rotation, those constant, targeted security audits... they are absolutely, unequivocally being used to build a paper trail against me. They keep showing me these logs, pointing to the screen and saying, "Look, it's just policy, it's just standard procedure," but I know what I'm looking at. 

Speaking of looking at screens, they recently upgraded all our monitors at work. We used to have these standard 24-inch Dell flat panels, but they brought in these massive 34-inch curved ultrawide displays. LG, I think. They're supposed to be better for your neck because you don't have to turn your head as much, but honestly, it just feels like you're sitting in the front row of an IMAX theater. 

I remember the first time I went to an IMAX theater. It was at the Smithsonian in Washington D.C. My wife and I took a trip there... oh, it must have been the late nineties. We saw this documentary about Mount Everest. The sheer scale of it was breathtaking. You really felt like you were standing on the edge of a crevasse. We spent three days just walking through the different museums. The Air and Space Museum was my favorite, of course. Seeing the actual Apollo 11 command module... Columbia, they called it. It's so much smaller in person than you'd imagine. To think three men spent eight days crammed in that tiny cone, flying all the way to the moon and back. The heat shield on the bottom was completely charred from re-entry. 

We actually bought a freeze-dried Neapolitan ice cream sandwich from the gift shop there. Astronaut ice cream, they called it. It came in this shiny foil pouch. Honestly, it tasted a bit like chalk, but it was the novelty of it, you know? 

But no, to answer your question... there's no evidence they could show me. Management can wave all the policy documents and audit logs they want in my face, but I know they're just using them to build a case against me. I've been trying to get someone to see it for over a year.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly states that no evidence could convince him that management is not building a case against him, demonstrating a fixed belief that is highly resistant to contradictory evidence.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the topic of work logs to new monitors, an IMAX theater, the Smithsonian, Apollo 11, and astronaut ice cream before finally returning to the original question.
